newsitem.title: INDIA: India approves 16.24 bln rupees foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: India approves 16.24 bln rupees foreign investment.

text.p: The Indian Industry Ministry said on Friday that it had approved 62 projects involving foreign direct investment (FDI) of 16.24 billion rupees ($456 million).
The projects, approved late on Thursday, cover industries ranging from petrochemicals to industrial gases to flowers.
They were expected to earn India foreign exchange of around 25 billion rupees over a period of five years, the ministry said in a statement.
The project involving the largest foreign investment -- -- 4.34 billion rupees -- was proposed by India's Haldia Petrochemicals Ltd.

U.S.-based financier George Soros owns a 25 percent stake in Haldia Petrochemicals through one of his fund managers, Purnendu Chatterjee. India's Tata group has a 8.33 percent stake, and the eastern state of West Bengal owns the rest.

The foreign investments will help the company to raise the annual capacity at Haldia's cracker plant to 420,000 tonnes from a planned 300,000. Its capacity could be further increased to 476,000 tonnes.
It was not known whether Soros would bring in fresh funds as part of the foreign investment. Company officials were not available for comment.
India's 13-party coalition government aims to bring in at least $10 billion of FDI into the country every year to overhaul and modernise the overburdened infrastructure.
French industrial gas firm Air Liquide was allowed to invest 1.0 billion rupees through its wholly-owned subsidiary, Air Liquide Holding India Pvt Ltd.
The Indian subsidiary will manufacture and distribute industrial, medical and other high purity gases.

TMT India was allowed to raise 1.6 billion rupees in foreign funds through a preference share issue. TMT will set up a 100 percent export-oriented unit in the southern state of Karnataka to cut 108 million flowers every year.
Korea's LG Chemicals Ltd was permitted to set up a 100 percent subsidiary with an investment of 3.50 billion rupees. The new company will make and sell organic and inorganic chemicals in India.
Cargill Asia Pacific Ltd was allowed to invest $25 million to permit an Indian subsidiary to enter into the flour milling business. Cargill currently processes seeds in India.
New Zealand's Fletcher Challenge was given permission to set up a wholly-owned subsidiary to start a concrete business in India. Fletcher will intiially invest 351 million rupees in its venture.
German pharmaceuticals firm Knoll AG can also now set up a 100 percent subsidiary at an investment of 107.5 million rupees.
